decisions.reason: Calderon et al. (2026) empirically re-analyzed original data from Yan, Sengupta, and Hong (2016, Experiment 3; DOI 10.1093/jcr/ucw045). Specifically, the authors requested and obtained Yan et al.'s Experiment 3 dataset, joined it with item-level comparative valence ratings from their BIF pretest, and re-estimated Yan et al.'s original social-distance effect on BIF responses while controlling for valence differences and testing the valence-by-distance interaction, finding that the social-distance effect was unchanged and the interaction was nonsignificant. Under the codebook, this same-data robustness re-analysis constitutes an actual reproduction of a specific published finding, distinct from merely adapting Yan et al.'s manipulation for the new-sample paradigmatic social-distance protocol (which had no suitable original BIF study) and from standalone pretest method development. The reference identity is explicitly backed by the primary text and reference list. It is genuinely absent from all three shipped rows and is not an alternate report of any of them: row 565 is Liberman and Trope (1998, Study 1; 10.1037/0022-3514.75.1.5, temporal distance, canonical mixed outcome preserved), row 566 is Fujita et al. (2006, Study 1; 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01698.x, spatial distance), and row 2494 is Wakslak et al. (2006, Study 1; 10.1037/0096-3445.135.4.641, likelihood manipulation). Per review instructions, record_type is coded as reproduction and outcome as cannot_be_determined, with the blind reproduction-axis proposals (not checked; robust) preserved only as proposals.

decisions.reason: For the direct replication of Liberman and Trope (1998, Study 1) on the 19-item BIF (omitting the original free-writing task and administering the 6 excluded BIF items on a separate page), the authors evaluated the replication against two explicit preregistered criteria—consistency in direction and consistency in magnitude—within an overall 'limited support' synthesis. They explicitly conclude that the temporal-distance replication effect was consistent in direction (d = 0.08, 95% CI [0.003, 0.16]; d = 0.12, 95% CI [0.06, 0.19] after valence adjustment) but inconsistent in magnitude with the original effect (d = 0.92, only 9% of the original size, with the replication CI upper bound excluding 0.92). Moreover, excluding the 21.5% comprehension-check failures caused the 95% CI to include zero (d = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.004, 0.17]), and item-level analyses showed 5 of 19 BIF items with CIs excluding zero in the predicted direction versus 5 of 19 in the opposite direction. Under the codebook, because the authors themselves present the Liberman & Trope (1998, Study 1) evidence as partly supporting (direction) and partly not supporting (magnitude and robustness) rather than as an unqualified success or the social-distance failure quoted in the shipped row, the outcome is 'mixed'.

decisions.location: Method - The effect of likelihood on the BIF, pp. 10-11 (chunk_index 46, chars 48844-49927; see also Follow-up questions - Self-rated mood, p. 11, chunk_index 49, and References, p. 29, chunk_index 123)
decisions.quote:
The effect of likelihood on the BIF
There was no suitable original study examining the effect
of likelihood on the BIF. Instead, we conducted a paradigmatic replication in which we adapted the design of
Fujita et al. (2006, Study 1) using an experimental manipulation of likelihood developed by Wakslak et al. (2006,
Study 1). Participants were asked to imagine that they
had been asked to help a friend move. Participants were
then told that the friend would be moving only if they
were offered a job they had applied for. In the highlikelihood condition, participants were told the friend
thought there was a 95% chance they would get the job.
In the low-likelihood condition, they were told that the
friend thought there was a 5% chance they would get
the job. Participants were then asked to fill out an
abridged nine-item BIF and to imagine performing the
activities in relation to the scenario of helping a friend
move. The nine BIF items were selected based on pretesting. In the pretest, an online sample (N = 183) rated
the relevance of the 25 BIF items to the scenario of
decisions.reason: The newly recovered full text of Wakslak, Trope, Liberman, and Alony (2006; DOI: 10.1037/0096-3445.135.4.641) establishes that Study 1 (N = 95) empirically tested and supported the hypothesis that low versus high event likelihood (5% vs. 95% probability across four scenarios, including relocating apartments contingent on a job offer) increases mental abstraction (fewer, broader object categories: M = 6.17 vs. 6.90, F(1, 92) = 4.70, p < .05, partial eta^2 = .049, unmediated by PANAS mood), while Study 7 (N = 26) found that low- versus high-probability scrambled-sentence primes increased abstract action identification on the 25-item BIF (t(24) = 2.19, p < .05, d = 0.89). Because object categorization failed computerized pretest validation (Mac Giolla et al., 2024) and Study 7 primed general probability concepts rather than manipulating event likelihood, Calderon et al. (2026) conducted a conceptual ('paradigmatic') replication (n = 2,936) that directly adapted Wakslak et al.'s (2006, Study 1) 5% versus 95% job-offer moving-scenario likelihood manipulation and PANAS mood check, substituting a pretested 9-item BIF measure of abstraction within Fujita et al.'s (2006, Study 1) helping-a-friend-move framing. Under the codebook, a changed dependent measure in a conceptual replication still re-tests the original empirical claim that low event likelihood increases mental abstraction, and no closer study in the replication chain is re-tested (Calderon et al., 2020 was excluded during screening). Since rows 565 and 566 cover only temporal and spatial originals and blind coding omitted this third target, shipped row 2494 is valid and unpaired.

decisions.reason: Evaluated specifically for the likelihood paradigmatic replication of Wakslak et al. (2006, Study 1) (n = 2,936 across k = 78 samples), the random-effects meta-analysis found a negligible, nonsignificant effect of event likelihood (5% distant vs. 95% close) on the 9-item BIF abstraction score: d = 0.03, 95% CI = [-0.05, 0.11] (unstandardized difference = 0.06 abstract choices, 95% CI = [-0.09, 0.22]; M = 4.62, SD = 2.01 in the low-likelihood condition vs. M = 4.53, SD = 2.04 in the high-likelihood condition), despite a strong manipulation-check effect (d = 1.98, 95% CI = [1.81, 2.14]). All nine individual BIF items had 95% CIs including zero, and the null result was unchanged when excluding comprehension-check failures or controlling for BIF response-option valence differences (b = 0.05, 95% CI = [-0.04, 0.13]; converted d = 0.03, 95% CI = [-0.02, 0.07]). In the Discussion, the authors explicitly conclude for the likelihood test that 'The replication effects for spatial distance and likelihood were small and had CIs that included zero, failing to support the original predictions.' Under the codebook, this explicit target-specific author conclusion of non-support codes as 'failed', confirming the shipped outcome.
